def: An MHC class I allele associated with autoimmune disease risk, including celiac disease, Graves disease and myasthenia gravis, typically inherited with HLA-DR3.
Thyroid enlargement in regions where dietary iodine is scarce. Low iodine impairs hormone synthesis, raising TSH and driving gland growth.
The tubes of each nephron that modify filtered fluid by reabsorbing and secreting solutes: proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct.
Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features (short stature, short fourth metacarpals, round face) with normal calcium and PTH. Occurs when the GNAS mutation is inherited from the father.
High blood pressure from reduced renal blood flow, most often renal artery stenosis. The kidney releases renin, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
Acute adrenal failure from bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, classically in meningococcal sepsis. Features shock, purpura and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
The methylated metabolite of norepinephrine, measured in plasma or urine. Raised levels suggest pheochromocytoma.
An enzyme that phosphorylates inositol phospholipids, activating the AKT pathway that promotes cell growth and survival. Insulin signaling and many cancers involve it.
Enlargement of an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease, with loss of cortisol feedback. Causes hyperpigmentation and mass effects.
Growth hormone insensitivity from a growth hormone receptor mutation. Short stature with high GH and low IGF-1.
An energy-sensing enzyme activated when AMP rises. It stimulates catabolic pathways and inhibits anabolic ones; metformin acts partly through it.
An SGLT2 inhibitor that blocks proximal tubule glucose reabsorption, causing glucosuria. Used for type 2 diabetes; risks include genital yeast infections and euglycemic ketoacidosis.
Diploid germ cells in the fetal ovary that divide by mitosis, then enter meiosis to become primary oocytes arrested in prophase I.
A protein made by Sertoli cells under FSH that binds testosterone in seminiferous tubules, maintaining high local androgen concentrations for spermatogenesis.
The second embryonic kidney, temporary in humans. Its duct becomes the Wolffian (mesonephric) duct, forming the male epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles.
A congenital uterine anomaly from incomplete fusion of the Mullerian ducts, giving a heart-shaped uterus with two horns. Linked to miscarriage and preterm labor.
An intraepithelial adenocarcinoma of apocrine-rich skin such as the vulva and perianal area, appearing as an itchy red scaly plaque with Paget cells.
Direct visualization of the uterine cavity with a thin scope passed through the cervix. Used to diagnose and treat polyps, fibroids and adhesions.
An ectopic pregnancy implanted in the fallopian tube, usually the ampulla. Risk of rupture and hemorrhage; presents with pain, bleeding and a positive hCG.
A benign ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor of theca cells that produces estrogen. Causes postmenopausal bleeding and endometrial hyperplasia.
Squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the skin, presenting as a red scaly plaque. It may follow arsenic exposure or sun damage.
Disappearance of disease without treatment. It is notably described with some cancers such as neuroblastoma and renal cell carcinoma.
A testicular sex cord-stromal tumor, usually benign, that may secrete estrogen causing gynecomastia. Histology shows tubules resembling seminiferous tubules.
A lysosomal enzyme that is high in prostate tissue. Prostatic acid phosphatase was an older prostate cancer marker; tartrate-resistant form marks hairy cell leukemia.
A tumor that is soft, fleshy and well circumscribed with lymphoid infiltrate. Medullary thyroid cancer arises from C cells and secretes calcitonin.
Breast cancer lacking estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2. Aggressive, common with BRCA1 mutations, and responds to chemotherapy rather than hormone therapy.
An embryonic outpouching of the hindgut. It becomes the urachus, which closes to form the median umbilical ligament.
Surgical removal of one or both ovaries.
A double fold of peritoneum draping over the uterus, fallopian tubes and ovaries. It contains the uterine vessels and the ureter runs beneath it.
The five long bones of the palm, between the carpal bones and fingers. Fifth metacarpal neck fracture is the boxer's fracture.
Molecules that draw cells such as neutrophils along a concentration gradient. Examples include C5a, IL-8, LTB4 and bacterial N-formylmethionine peptides.
The forebrain structure at the base of the frontal lobe where cranial nerve I axons synapse. It passes smell information to the olfactory cortex without a thalamic relay.
An abnormal chromosome where one arm is duplicated and the other lost, forming a mirror image. Isochromosome Xq is seen in Turner syndrome.
The calcium phosphate crystal that forms the mineral of bone and teeth.
Bone loss after menopause from estrogen deficiency, which increases osteoclast activity. Causes vertebral compression and hip fractures.
A transcription factor that promotes inflammatory gene expression. It is held inactive by IkB and activated by TNF and toll-like receptors.
The water channel inserted in the collecting duct apical membrane under ADH (V2 receptor) action. Defects cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
An intracellular receptor that binds cortisol and acts as a transcription factor, regulating metabolism and suppressing inflammation.
The round ligament of the liver, the fibrous remnant of the fetal umbilical vein. It runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament.
Prescribing a drug for an indication, dose or population not approved by regulators.
An antacid that neutralizes stomach acid. Can cause constipation and hypophosphatemia, and accumulates in kidney failure.
A sulfonamide that is the active metabolite of sulfasalazine, which is cleaved by gut bacteria to sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid.
An inactivated X chromosome seen as a dense mass in the nucleus of female cells. Normal females have one; XXX has two.
A pyrimidine base in DNA that pairs with adenine. Made from uracil by methylation using thymidylate synthase.
A five-carbon sugar that forms the backbone of RNA and ATP. It has a hydroxyl at the 2' position, which deoxyribose lacks.
The main replicating enzyme in prokaryotes, extending DNA with 5' to 3' polymerase and 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading.
A prokaryotic enzyme that removes RNA primers via 5' to 3' exonuclease activity and fills the gap with DNA.
A DNA region upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase and transcription factors bind to begin transcription. Eukaryotic examples include the TATA box.
An insertion or deletion of nucleotides not divisible by three, shifting the reading frame and altering all downstream codons. Often produces a premature stop codon.
Circular DNA in mitochondria, inherited only from the mother. Mutations cause heteroplasmic mitochondrial diseases such as MELAS and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.
Proteins such as TFIID that assemble at promoters with RNA polymerase II to start transcription.
A protein motif that coordinates a zinc ion to fold into a DNA-binding loop. It is common in transcription factors and steroid hormone receptors.
Transcription factors with a conserved DNA-binding motif encoded by homeobox genes, including HOX genes, which pattern the body axis during development.
The enzyme that transcribes most ribosomal RNA genes (28S, 18S, 5.8S) in the nucleolus.
Complexes of RNA with proteins, such as ribosomes, snRNPs in the spliceosome and telomerase.
RNA that is not translated to protein, including rRNA, tRNA, microRNA, snRNA and long noncoding RNA. Many regulate gene expression.
The small eukaryotic ribosomal subunit. It binds mRNA and initiator tRNA to begin translation.
Chemical changes to a protein after translation, such as phosphorylation, glycosylation, ubiquitination and proteolytic cleavage, that alter its function or location.
A ribonucleoprotein that binds the signal peptide of a new protein and pauses translation, guiding the ribosome to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
A six-carbon sugar and epimer of glucose. Mannose-6-phosphate tags lysosomal enzymes; defects cause I-cell disease.
A membrane vesicle that sorts material taken up by endocytosis. Its acidic contents allow receptors to separate from ligands before recycling or lysosomal degradation.
A protein that forms a lattice coat on vesicles in receptor-mediated endocytosis and Golgi trafficking.
An intermediate filament protein of mesenchymal cells such as fibroblasts, endothelium and muscle. It is a marker of sarcomas and mesenchymal tumors.
The stage of embryonic development, weeks 3 to 8, when organs form. Teratogens during this period cause major malformations.
The mineralized tissue forming the bulk of a tooth beneath enamel, made by odontoblasts. Defective in dentinogenesis imperfecta.
The main collagen of hyaline cartilage, the vitreous humor and the nucleus pulposus.
The gelatinous center of an intervertebral disc, a remnant of the notochord. Herniation through the annulus fibrosus compresses nerve roots.
A minor fibrillar collagen that regulates fibril assembly. Defects cause classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
A yellow, elastic ligament connecting adjacent vertebral laminae. It is pierced during lumbar puncture and epidural anesthesia.
The soluble precursor of elastin, secreted and cross-linked by lysyl oxidase.
DNA synthesized from mRNA by reverse transcriptase. Lacks introns and is used for cloning and expression.
Short nucleic acid sequences that supply the 3' end where DNA polymerase begins synthesis. In PCR they flank the target.
Mature bone cells embedded in lacunae within mineralized matrix. They sense mechanical stress and regulate bone remodeling.
The plasma membrane of a muscle cell. It invaginates as T-tubules to carry the action potential inward.
A 7q11.23 deletion including the elastin gene. Features elfin facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia, outgoing personality and intellectual disability.
A group of alleles on one chromosome that are inherited together, such as an HLA haplotype.
A statistic for genetic linkage: the log of the odds that two loci are linked. A score of 3 or more supports linkage.
Extra fingers or toes. It appears in trisomy 13, Bardet-Biedl syndrome and as an isolated trait.
A thin filament protein that covers myosin-binding sites on actin at rest. Calcium-bound troponin moves it aside to allow contraction.
A regulatory protein of the sarcoplasmic reticulum that inhibits SERCA calcium uptake. Phosphorylation by PKA relieves inhibition, speeding cardiac relaxation.
Disorders of the aortic valve, including stenosis and regurgitation. Causes include calcific degeneration, bicuspid valve and rheumatic fever.
The unpaired artery from the aorta at T12 that supplies the foregut: stomach, liver, spleen and upper pancreas and duodenum. It divides into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.
Calcification of the media of medium-sized arteries, forming rings without luminal narrowing. Found in older adults and diabetes.
Rod-like bundles of contractile filaments within a muscle cell, composed of repeating sarcomeres.
Infarction of the heart's bottom surface, usually from right coronary artery occlusion. ST elevation is in leads II, III and aVF; may involve the right ventricle and cause bradycardia.
Narrowing of the muscular right ventricular outflow below the pulmonary valve, as in tetralogy of Fallot.
Narrowing of the path from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery, as in pulmonary stenosis or tetralogy of Fallot.
A branch of the subclavian artery running along the inner chest wall. The left internal thoracic artery is the preferred graft to the LAD in bypass surgery.
A class IB sodium channel blocker (lidocaine analog). Used orally for ventricular arrhythmias and neuropathic pain.
A class IB antiarrhythmic related to lidocaine, now rarely used because of pulmonary fibrosis and blood dyscrasias.
A class IC sodium channel blocker for supraventricular arrhythmias. Contraindicated after myocardial infarction (CAST trial) because of proarrhythmia.
A glycosaminoglycan in skin, vessels and heart valves. Accumulates in Hurler and Hunter syndromes (mucopolysaccharidoses).
An anaerobic gram-positive rod causing spontaneous gas gangrene, usually in patients with colon cancer or neutropenia.
A genus of small gram-negative coccobacilli. A. actinomycetemcomitans (Aggregatibacter) causes periodontitis and endocarditis (HACEK).
Dilated cardiomyopathy from chronic heavy alcohol use, causing reduced ejection fraction and heart failure. May improve with abstinence.
The wall between the left and right atria. Defects include atrial septal defect and patent foramen ovale.
A procedure using a catheter to destroy small areas of cardiac tissue by heat or cold that cause abnormal rhythm, as in atrial fibrillation and Wolff-Parkinson-White.
A gray-white ring at the periphery of the cornea from lipid deposition. Common in older adults; in the young it suggests hyperlipidemia.
A small volume of serous fluid between the pericardial layers that lubricates the heart. Excess causes effusion or tamponade.
The motor domain subunit of myosin that binds actin and hydrolyzes ATP. Beta-MHC mutations cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Ultrasound of the heart from a probe in the esophagus. It gives clearer images of the atria, valves and aorta than the chest wall approach.
The vein continuing from the axillary vein, passing over the first rib to join the internal jugular. A common site for central venous access.
A plasma enzyme that esterifies cholesterol on HDL, trapping it in the particle core. Deficiency causes corneal opacities and anemia.
A statin that inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, lowering LDL cholesterol. Side effects include myopathy and liver enzyme elevation.
A fibrate that activates PPAR-alpha, lowering triglycerides. Can cause myopathy and gallstones.
A fibrate that activates PPAR-alpha, lowering triglycerides. Risks include myopathy when combined with statins, and gallstones.
Organelles in type II pneumocytes that store and secrete surfactant. Also found in epidermal keratinocytes.
The maximum volume exhaled after a full inhalation. It equals inspiratory reserve volume plus tidal volume plus expiratory reserve volume.
Muscles between the ribs. External ones raise the ribs in inspiration; internal and innermost aid forced exhalation.
Ring-shaped molecules that bind metals, forming heme when iron is added. Their buildup causes porphyria.
A topical ester local anesthetic. A cause of methemoglobinemia.
Breathing 100% oxygen at above normal pressure. Used for carbon monoxide poisoning, decompression sickness and gas gangrene.
Sensory endings in airway smooth muscle that detect lung inflation and signal via the vagus nerve to end inspiration (Hering-Breuer reflex).
Unconscious mental processes that protect against anxiety or unacceptable impulses, such as denial, repression, projection and sublimation.
A localized tumor of monoclonal plasma cells, in bone or soft tissue, which can progress to multiple myeloma.
The gland in the upper outer orbit that produces tears. Its ducts open into the conjunctival sac.
Noncaseating granulomas in the lungs and hilar lymph nodes, causing cough, dyspnea and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
A sympathetic ganglion formed by fused inferior cervical and first thoracic ganglia. Damage or blockade causes Horner syndrome.
A vein along the right side of the vertebral column that drains the posterior thorax into the superior vena cava. It provides collateral flow if the inferior vena cava is blocked.
A platelet integrin receptor that binds fibrinogen, linking platelets together. Abciximab, eptifibatide and tirofiban block it; deficiency is Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
Removal of a patient's plasma and replacement with donor plasma or albumin. Used to remove autoantibodies or toxins in Guillain-Barre, TTP and myasthenic crisis.
The large eukaryotic ribosomal subunit, which contains the peptidyl transferase activity that forms peptide bonds.
A coagulation test that measures the extrinsic and common pathways. Prolonged by warfarin and vitamin K deficiency.
Hageman factor, which starts the intrinsic coagulation pathway on contact with surfaces. Deficiency prolongs aPTT without bleeding.
X-linked recessive factor IX deficiency, also called Christmas disease. Causes hemarthroses and prolonged aPTT.
Inherited thrombophilia from reduced protein S, a cofactor of protein C. Causes venous thromboembolism and warfarin-induced skin necrosis.
Fatty acids with fewer than six carbons, produced by colonic bacterial fermentation of fiber. Butyrate is the main fuel of colonocytes.
A sugar alcohol made from galactose by aldose reductase. It accumulates in galactosemia, causing cataracts.
The enzyme that converts galactose-1-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate. Its deficiency causes classic galactosemia.
Coenzyme Q, a lipid-soluble electron carrier in the mitochondrial respiratory chain that transfers electrons from complexes I and II to complex III.
The cytochrome bc1 complex of the electron transport chain, passing electrons from ubiquinol to cytochrome c. Antimycin A inhibits it.
A heme protein in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, a part of complex III.
A compound that oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which binds cyanide. Used with thiosulfate as a cyanide poisoning antidote.
An enzyme that removes glycogen branches during breakdown. Deficiency causes Cori disease (type III glycogen storage disease).
Lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase that breaks down glycogen. Deficiency causes Pompe disease with cardiomegaly and muscle weakness.
Enzymes that break bonds by adding water, such as lipases, proteases and lysosomal acid hydrolases.
Inherited thrombophilia from reduced protein C, which inactivates factors Va and VIIIa. Causes venous thrombosis and warfarin-induced skin necrosis.
CT scanning with a continuously rotating tube while the patient moves through the scanner, giving fast volumetric images.
Hives lasting longer than six weeks. Often autoimmune, with no external trigger.
The enzyme that converts arachidonic acid to leukotrienes. Zileuton inhibits it in asthma.
A cysteinyl leukotriene causing bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion and increased vascular permeability in asthma. Montelukast blocks its receptor.
An enzyme that cleaves DNA. DNase breaks down DNA, as in pulmonary secretions in cystic fibrosis (dornase alfa).
An angiotensin II receptor blocker for hypertension and heart failure. It does not cause cough but is teratogenic and may raise potassium.
A contact-activation protein that anchors factor XII and prekallikrein and releases bradykinin.
A kidney structure with macula densa cells, juxtaglomerular cells and mesangial cells. It senses sodium and pressure, and releases renin.
Blockage of urine flow in the ureter by stones, tumor or stricture, causing hydronephrosis and flank pain.
Movement of water between body compartments, driven by osmotic and hydrostatic forces.
The plasma flow reaching functional kidney tissue, estimated by PAH clearance. Dividing by one minus hematocrit gives renal blood flow.
Abnormally low blood protein, usually from loss in nephrotic syndrome, liver failure or malnutrition. It reduces oncotic pressure and causes edema.
A cholinergic agonist resistant to acetylcholinesterase, acting on muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Used in glaucoma and to induce miosis.
The chromosome carrying the Huntington gene (HTT), polycystic kidney disease 2 and the gene for achondroplasia (FGFR3).
Tamm-Horsfall protein, the most abundant urinary protein, secreted by the thick ascending limb. It forms casts and protects against urinary tract infection.
The first and nonfunctional embryonic kidney in humans, regressing by week 4.
Basic fibroblast growth factor, which promotes angiogenesis and wound healing.
Healing where epithelial cells migrate across a wound to restore the surface.
Cells of the glomerulus that support the capillary loops and regulate filtration. They phagocytose immune complexes, which are deposited in IgA nephropathy.
Splitting of polarized light into two rays by an anisotropic material. Under polarized light, gout crystals are negatively birefringent and pseudogout crystals positively birefringent.
The most common pediatric liver cancer, raising alpha-fetoprotein. Associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis.
Urothelial carcinoma, the most common bladder cancer, linked to smoking and aniline dyes. Causes painless hematuria.
Synthetic dyes with a nitrogen double bond. Some are carcinogens associated with bladder cancer.
A mutation that gives a protein new or enhanced activity, as in oncogene activation. Typically dominant.
The cytoplasmic enzyme that interconverts CO2 and bicarbonate. Mutations cause osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis.
A mesh tape placed under the urethra to support it. Used to treat stress urinary incontinence.
Weak detrusor muscle contraction causing incomplete emptying and overflow incontinence. Seen with diabetic neuropathy or spinal injury.
Lipid mediators (PGE1, PGE2) that cause vasodilation and fever, protect gastric mucosa and keep the ductus arteriosus open.
A cytoplasmic pathway generating NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate. G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme.
A five-carbon sugar such as ribose or deoxyribose, which forms the backbone of nucleic acids.
An enzyme that regenerates reduced glutathione using NADPH, protecting red cells from oxidative damage.
A cytosolic enzyme that cleaves citrate into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate to supply acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis.
A multifunctional cytosolic enzyme that builds palmitate from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA using NADPH.
A 20-carbon omega-6 fatty acid released from membranes by phospholipase A2. It is the precursor of prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes.
Cholesterol carried by low-density lipoprotein, which deposits in artery walls and promotes atherosclerosis.
The rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, which converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate. Statins inhibit it.
Chemicals that drive inflammation, such as histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, bradykinin and cytokines.
A cholesterol-rich lipoprotein formed from VLDL and cleared by LDL receptors. It carries cholesterol to peripheral tissues.
Lipids built on a sphingosine backbone, including ceramide, sphingomyelin and gangliosides. Lysosomal storage diseases such as Tay-Sachs and Gaucher involve them.
An amino alcohol that forms the backbone of sphingolipids. Joined to a fatty acid it makes ceramide.
The lysosomal enzyme that degrades GM2 ganglioside. Deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease.
A lysosomal enzyme that removes N-acetylhexosamine residues from glycolipids. Defects cause Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff diseases.
The lysosomal enzyme that cleaves glucose from glucocerebroside. Deficiency causes Gaucher disease.
An enzyme that cleaves galactose from glycolipids. Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease; beta-galactosidase deficiency causes GM1 gangliosidosis.
A lysosomal enzyme that removes sulfate groups from sulfatides. Arylsulfatase A deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy.
A diet limiting protein, used in advanced kidney disease and urea cycle disorders to reduce nitrogen waste.
An artificial sweetener containing phenylalanine, which must be avoided by patients with phenylketonuria.
An enzyme that makes the folate form used by methionine synthase. Mutations raise homocysteine.
Excessive forward curvature of the thoracic spine, causing a rounded upper back. Seen in osteoporosis and Scheuermann disease.
Otolith organs of the inner ear that sense linear acceleration and head tilt. The utricle detects horizontal motion and the saccule vertical.
A purine salvage enzyme. Deficiency causes toxic metabolite buildup in T cells, leading to severe T-cell immunodeficiency.
Inflammation of the lips, with cracking and scaling. Angular cheilitis occurs at the mouth corners, and is associated with riboflavin or iron deficiency.
A heme synthesis enzyme, also called hydroxymethylbilane synthase. Deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria.
A heme synthesis intermediate formed by uroporphyrinogen III synthase. Deficiency of the synthase causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria.
A heme synthesis enzyme. Its deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda, with blistering skin on sun exposure.
The mitochondrial enzyme that inserts iron into protoporphyrin to make heme. It is inhibited by lead and deficient in erythropoietic protoporphyria.
A green pigment from heme breakdown, reduced to bilirubin. It gives bruises a green color.
An alpha-2 agonist eye drop that lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous humor production. Used in glaucoma.
A drug that irreversibly blocks VMAT, depleting catecholamine stores in nerve terminals. Used as an antihypertensive; can cause depression.
A cardioselective beta-1 blocker used for hypertension and heart failure.
Narrowing of the pathway from the left ventricle to the aorta, as in aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
A tetramer of four beta chains formed when three alpha-globin genes are deleted (HbH disease). It has poor oxygen delivery and causes hemolytic anemia.
The most common nucleotide or amino acid at each position of a set of related sequences, such as the TATA box.
The skull's face-forming bones, including the maxilla, mandible, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine, vomer and inferior concha.
The most abundant RNA, forming the structural and catalytic core of the ribosome. It is made by RNA polymerase I in the nucleolus.
Blood flow in arterioles, capillaries and venules, where exchange takes place.
CD55, a GPI-anchored protein that protects red cells from complement. Its absence causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
A genus of mosquito that transmits Plasmodium, the cause of malaria.
Cuts in one or both DNA strands, from radiation or chemicals. Double-strand breaks are repaired by nonhomologous end joining or homologous recombination.
A polyclonal antibody against human T cells, given for transplant rejection and aplastic anemia.
A scoring system estimating mortality in intensive care patients from physiologic variables.
The embryonic rhombencephalon, which forms the pons, medulla and cerebellum.
A cluster of neuron cell bodies where preganglionic fibers synapse onto postganglionic neurons of the sympathetic or parasympathetic system.
Gaps in the myelin sheath of an axon where voltage-gated sodium channels cluster, allowing saltatory conduction.
Progressive joint destruction from loss of pain and proprioception due to neuropathy. Common in diabetes, tabes dorsalis and syringomyelia.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, an inherited peripheral nerve disorder causing distal weakness, foot deformities and sensory loss.
A herniation of meninges, but not the spinal cord, through a vertebral defect, forming a cystic sac.
Precursor cells in bone marrow that mature into monocytes. They are the leukemic cells in acute monocytic leukemia (M5).
Bone marrow precursors of megakaryocytes. They proliferate in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (M7), associated with Down syndrome.
Antibodies that react with antigens from unrelated species. In infectious mononucleosis, they agglutinate sheep or horse red cells (Monospot test).
A nuclear receptor for vitamin A-derived retinoic acid that regulates gene expression. It is fused with PML in acute promyelocytic leukemia, which responds to all-trans retinoic acid.
